findings.title: Filesystem links can redirect archive access outside the repository
findings.description: The archive root and run directories are constructed lexically and then passed directly to filesystem APIs. No component is resolved and checked for containment, and symbolic links, junctions, or other reparse points are not rejected. An attacker able to control repository filesystem contents can place a link at the archive root, month, run, or archive-file level and cause create, append, or read operations to follow it outside the intended `.quality/run-history` boundary. Create-only mode prevents replacement of an existing destination file but does not prevent creation in a redirected directory; append and read operations also follow redirected paths.
findings.recommendation: Resolve and validate the real filesystem target beneath a trusted canonical archive root before every operation, reject symbolic links and reparse points in all path components, and use no-follow or handle-relative filesystem operations where supported. Consider storing security-sensitive archive data outside repository-controlled paths.

findings.title: Unbounded archive loading permits resource-exhaustion denial of service
findings.description: Archive files and collections are read and deserialized without limits on file size, line length, record count, or aggregate allocation. `LoadRun` reads an entire file into memory, `LoadAttempts` materializes every matching file and its contents, and line-based loaders accumulate every record into a list. A repository contributor or compromised process can create oversized or numerous archive records that consume excessive memory and CPU whenever these public loading methods are invoked.
findings.recommendation: Set explicit maximum file sizes, JSON-line lengths, record counts, and aggregate bytes before deserialization. Stream records where possible, reject oversized files before reading them, and apply cancellation or processing budgets to archive enumeration.
